analysis.one_liner: Gives free emergency insulin to uninsured and underinsured people, paid by fees and price-spike taxes on insulin makers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to two House committees in May 2023, it sat in the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal grant program so states, tribes, and tribal organizations can issue insulin cards giving uninsured and underinsured people a 7-day emergency supply within days, followed by 90-day supplies, at no cost. The program would be funded entirely by annual fees on insulin manufacturers, charged by market share. It would also impose an excise tax on manufacturers whose insulin prices spike faster than inflation, and would cut the market exclusivity period for biological drugs from 12 to 7 years to open the door to cheaper copies.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured people who need insulin, especially those in high-deductible health plans, would get insulin at no cost through card programs run by states, tribes, and tribal organizations. Amounts paid by the program would count toward their insurance deductibles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured people who need insulin

how_it_helps.text: States, Indian tribes, and tribal organizations would receive grants to run insulin card programs; a person applying would get an initial card valid for a roughly 7-day supply of insulin within 5 business days, and, if found eligible, a card for a roughly 90-day supply within 12 business days, with prescriptions filled at pharmacies at no cost to the individual.
For underinsured people in high-deductible health plans, payments the program makes to pharmacies for their insulin must be counted toward the plan's deductible or other out-of-pocket requirements.
The program would be funded by annual fees on insulin manufacturers, 2024 through 2028, sized to equal the total cost of the grant program and divided among manufacturers by market share.

An excise tax would apply when an insulin price rises faster than inflation: 50% of the extra revenue for smaller spikes, 75% for 15-20% spikes, and 100% for spikes of 20% or more, with exemptions only for verifiable input-cost increases.
The market exclusivity period for biological drug products would be cut from 12 years to 7 years, allowing competing biosimilar insulins to reach the market sooner.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would bear the annual fees and the price-spike excise tax, and would face shorter exclusivity for biological products. States, tribes, and tribal organizations would have to contribute $1 in matching funds for every $3 in federal grant money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insulin manufacturers, plus state matching funds

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes prices paid under the insulin card program from the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program's 'best price' and average manufacturer price calculations, which weakens one of the main tools that pushes drug prices down across Medicaid.
The grant program sunsets 5 years after enactment, and states must put up non-federal matching funds of at least $1 for every $3 of federal money, which could limit participation by poorer states.

The excise tax reaches up to 100% of the revenue from a price spike, a penalty steep enough that even supporters would need to defend it against the argument that it could discourage new insulin investment; the bill counters this only by allowing exemptions for documented input-cost increases.
The fee only pays for the assistance program itself; it does nothing for insured people whose insulin costs are already above what the card program would cover.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the narrow population it targets - uninsured people and people in high-deductible plans who need insulin - the benefit is direct and immediate, and making manufacturers fund the program is a reasonable design. The carve-out from Medicaid's best-price rules and the 5-year sunset are real weaknesses, but the core trade is straightforward: a working assistance program in exchange for fees and a price-spike penalty on the manufacturers who profit from high insulin prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on May 9, 2023, with Rep. Dean Phillips as its sole cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and to the House Ways and Means Committee, splitting its provisions across two committees.
On May 12, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health of Energy and Commerce, and again on December 17, 2024 - the last action of its life.
No committee vote, hearing on the bill itself, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill's complete action history ends with the subcommittee referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill; it would have to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they keep the 12-year exclusivity, pay no program fees, and face no excise tax on price increases faster than inflation. Insurers and pharmacies are unaffected, and uninsured diabetics continue to face cash prices for insulin.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin manufacturers, whose fees and price-spike taxes never took effect

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a markup or vote; its Health Subcommittee held the referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral for the provisions in its jurisdiction and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded on the bill, so no roll-call split exists; its only two sponsors, Angie Craig and Dean Phillips of Minnesota, were both Democrats.

industries.note: They would pay annual fees equal to the program's cost, divided by market share, and an excise tax of 50% to 100% of the revenue from price increases above inflation. The bill does soften this by exempting program prices from Medicaid's best-price rebate calculations.
Cutting market exclusivity from 12 years to 7 would let biosimilar competitors reach the market sooner, reducing the years of monopoly pricing on biologics including insulin.
The card program pays pharmacies for filling insulin prescriptions for eligible people at no charge to the patient, bringing them new reimbursed volume.
They would have to count the program's payments toward members' deductibles, which helps their enrollees but reduces the amount of deductible spending those members bear directly.
